Photography club note - Nilesh (teacher in charge), Class 11
The brief this month was "a week in my life," seven photos. Samir submitted seven selfies: cricket ground, birthday cake, beach, new shoes, each with a wide grin and bright edits.
They were technically good. But when the club looked at them, one student said, "Your life looks like an advert."
Samir laughed it off. Then, after everyone left, he showed me an eighth photo he hadn't submitted: his desk at night, a pile of maths papers, a cold cup of tea, a lamp.
"That's most of my week," he said. "But nobody posts that."
I told him the seven were honest too, just chosen. The eighth was also chosen, just differently. Both are a presented self.
He asked if he could submit all eight. The club voted the desk photo the most striking of the month.

qa.q: How many selfies did Samir submit at first?
qa.a: Samir submitted seven selfies.

qa.q: What might Samir have been feeling when he showed the eighth photo?
qa.a: He seemed a little vulnerable and relieved to show a truer side, after laughing off the "advert" comment.

qa.q: What did Nilesh help Samir understand?
qa.a: That every photo is chosen and framed, so both the bright selfies and the desk photo present a self rather than the full picture.

qa.q: How might the club members have felt seeing the desk photo?
qa.a: They probably found it relatable and striking, since most of their weeks also include tired desks that nobody posts.

grounding: The teacher's note shows a teenager curating photos to present a bright self, and recognising posted images as chosen, not a full picture.

Saturday
Took forty-three selfies before the farewell party to get one good one. Forty-three! In the end I posted the one where my hair looked right and the light hid the pimple. Caption: "last day, best day ✨".
Honestly, the last day wasn't the best day. I cried in the bathroom because I'm going to miss everyone.
Then Nilesh posted a meme of our whole class: our faces stuck onto the cast of that old college film, with our class teacher as the principal. I laughed so hard. It felt more like us than any selfie.
It made me think. My selfie shows a girl who had a perfect day. The meme shows a class that's a bit of a mess and loves each other. The meme's closer to the truth.
Might post the bathroom-crying version next year. Maybe.
- Binita

qa.a: Binita took forty-three selfies.

qa.q: What was Binita feeling on the last day?
qa.a: Binita felt sad and nostalgic, crying in the bathroom because of missing everyone, even though the post said "best day."

qa.q: What would you advise Binita about posting next year?
qa.a: Choose images that feel true, like the class meme, and remember that a post is always a chosen version, not the whole day.

qa.q: How might Nilesh's classmates have seen his meme?
qa.a: They probably felt amused and connected, seeing their messy, affectionate class in a shared joke.

grounding: The diary shows a teenager curating a selfie that hides mixed feelings, and a group meme signalling humour and belonging.

Dear Shalini,
Guess what's still in my phone cover? The ticket from the last film we saw before you moved to Bhopal. Screen 2, row F, seats 11 and 12. It's faded now.
Yesterday Rehan grabbed my phone, saw it, and announced to the whole bench, "Samir has a date ticket!" Everyone howled. I didn't explain. It felt like explaining would make it smaller.
But you know what it is. It's the day we laughed so much at the terrible film that the usher came to shush us. It's the last normal day before you left.
Nobody else can see that in a piece of paper. They see a ticket and make up a story.
Only Farida asked, later, quietly, "What's the ticket about?" I told her. She said, "That's nice. I keep a bus pass like that."
Write back soon.
Samir

Pradeep, you asked about my watch on this podcast, so okay. I'm Thomas, and everyone at school thinks it's a vintage fashion thing. It's old, brass, scratched, and honestly it doesn't even work. Stopped at twenty past four.

It was my grandfather's. He wore it every day when he drove the school bus in Kottayam. After he passed, my grandmother gave it to me and said, "He'd want it on a wrist, not in a drawer."

I don't mind people thinking it's fashion. But the best thing anyone did was my coach. He just asked, "Tell me about the watch." And I did.

I'm Kalyani, and I share a hostel room with Gargi. On her wrist she wears a faded, fraying friendship bracelet, red and yellow threads. She never takes it off, not even for swimming.
For weeks I assumed it was from an ex. The way she twisted it when she was on calls home, I thought she missed someone. I even joked once, "Still thinking about him?" She just smiled and didn't answer.
Then one night I asked properly. "Gargi, the bracelet. What's the story? You don't have to tell."
She looked at it. "My little sister made it when I left for hostel. She was seven. She said I'm not allowed to take it off until I come home for good."
I felt so silly about the joke. I said sorry.
Now when she twists it on calls home, I know she's missing her sister.

qa.a: She was seven.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling after hearing the bracelet's story?
qa.a: Kalyani felt silly and sorry about the earlier joke, and touched to learn the bracelet was a link to Gargi's little sister.

qa.q: What did Kalyani learn about asking?
qa.a: That curiosity, asking gently and saying "you don't have to tell," works better than assuming and joking about an object's meaning.

qa.q: How might Gargi have felt when Kalyani joked about an ex?
qa.a: She may have felt a little misunderstood, but chose not to explain until Kalyani asked properly.

In the boys' school in Pune, Tushar had started arriving late. Ishita Ma'am, his class teacher, noticed his hair was always perfectly set, and he'd sometimes leave class to check it in the washroom mirror.
On Wednesday he arrived at the second period, red-eyed. At lunch she asked him to help carry books to the staff room.
"You've been late a lot. Is everything okay?"
He stared at the floor. "My hair wouldn't go right. I look horrible compared to everyone online. I couldn't come like that."
Ishita Ma'am didn't laugh. "How you style yourself is your choice, and it's fine to care. But it doesn't decide what you're worth. You're the best debater in 9B."
He gave a small smile.
She didn't stop there. That evening she phoned his parents to share what she'd noticed, and they agreed to keep an eye on it together and to talk to the counsellor if it went on.

So, Sahil, you asked about filters on this show. I'm Ojas, and last year I couldn't post a single photo without editing my face. Smoother skin, sharper chin, even my eyes bigger.
Then it went further. I wouldn't go out if my hair was wrong. I stopped playing football because I sweated and looked "bad." I checked mirrors everywhere.
My mother noticed. Not the first day. But after a few weeks of me skipping things, she sat with me one night and said, "You seem really unhappy. Is it about how you look?"
I cried, honestly. She didn't say "don't be silly." She said, "You can dress how you want. But you are not your face." And the next week she came with me to the school counsellor.
It got better slowly. I still like nice hair. I just don't cancel my life for it.

Teacher's note - Lokesh, Class 10 social science, Monday
During a discussion on choice and culture, one student, meaning well, said Vidya must "have to" wear her hijab. Vidya went quiet, then answered calmly: "Nobody forces me. My mother doesn't even wear one. I chose it in Class 8. It's my faith and, honestly, I like how it looks."
Another student, Parminder, said her own turban was partly faith and partly her grandfather's wish. A third said she wears a bindi for style some days and not others.
I asked the class what they noticed. One boy said, "The same thing can mean different things to different people."
I told them that's exactly why we should ask, not assume. Afterwards the first student apologised to Vidya, and Vidya said, "It's fine. Ask me anything. Just don't tell me what it means for me."

qa.q: When did Vidya choose to wear her hijab?
qa.a: She chose it in Class 8.

qa.q: What might Vidya have felt when told she must "have to" wear it?
qa.a: Vidya probably felt misunderstood and a little hurt, going quiet before calmly explaining it was her own choice.

qa.q: What did Lokesh do to turn the moment into learning?
qa.a: He let students share their own reasons and asked what they noticed, helping the class see that the same item can mean different things.

qa.q: How might the student who apologised have seen the hijab before the discussion?
qa.a: That student seemed to assume it was always imposed, without asking what it meant to Vidya.

grounding: The teacher's note shows that items like a hijab, turban or bindi can be faith, family expectation, choice or style, and that nobody should assume their meaning.

At the swimming pool changing room today, Vishal saw my janeu and said, "Whoa, didn't know you were so religious."
I didn't know what to say. Am I? I wear it because Papa did my thread ceremony last year and Dadaji cried with happiness. I don't pray every day. Some days I forget it's there. Some days I touch it before exams.
So I said, "It's complicated. Family, mostly. And a bit mine."
Vishal nodded. Then he held up his wrist. "This kara is from my friend in Ludhiana. I'm not Sikh. It just means he's my brother."
We looked at each other and laughed. Two bits of thread and metal, and we'd both assumed about the other.
I think I'll keep wearing it. I'll figure out what it means for me later.
- Sachin

Coach's note - Harish, school band, Friday
Sahil turned up to rehearsal with bright blue hair. His mother had phoned me in the morning, worried. She asked if something was wrong, if he was "falling in with a bad crowd."
I watched him closely all week. He was on time, practised his drum part more than anyone, and joked with the juniors. The only change was the hair, and a new black band T-shirt.
When I asked him, he shrugged. "The drummer in my favourite band has blue hair. Also I wanted to see how I'd look. I might change it next month."
I called his mother back. I told her he seemed happy, focused and part of the group, and that trying a new look at sixteen is normal. We agreed to keep an eye on the bigger things, like sleep, mood and friends, not the colour.
Next week, three band members turned up with blue streaks.

qa.q: What colour was Sahil's hair?
qa.a: Bright blue.

qa.q: What was Sahil's mother feeling when she phoned?
qa.a: She was worried and anxious, afraid the blue hair meant something was wrong or that Sahil was falling in with a bad crowd.

qa.q: What did Harish do that helped?
qa.a: He watched Sahil's behaviour for a week, asked him directly, and reassured his mother that the hair looked like experimentation, while agreeing to watch mood and sleep.

qa.q: What would change if Sahil's mother had banned the hair colour straight away?
qa.a: Sahil might have felt judged and less willing to talk, over what was really just a trial and a sign of belonging to the band.

grounding: The coach's note shows a teenager experimenting with hair colour for belonging and self-exploration, and adults not treating it as proof of trouble.

The football derby in Kolkata was sold out, and the stands were a sea of red and yellow. Kashish had painted her cheeks and was chanting louder than her aunt Jyoti had ever heard her.
"Who is this girl?" Jyoti laughed. At home Kashish barely spoke above a whisper.
In the sixty-eighth minute, a disputed goal. The crowd around them surged. Someone threw a plastic bottle. Then another. A group behind them started shoving towards the railings, and the chant turned into something ugly.
Kashish felt the pull of it, the anger buzzing through everyone.
Jyoti grabbed her hand. "We're leaving. Now."
"But the match!"
"The match isn't worth a crush."
They edged along the row, away from the shoving, and out of the nearest exit. Outside, Kashish's heart was still hammering. "I've never shouted like that."
"Crowds do that," Jyoti said. "That's why you keep one eye on the exit."

qa.q: What was Kashish feeling when the crowd turned angry?

qa.q: Which choice was wise, and why?

I still remember my first Ganpati procession without my parents. I was fifteen, with my cousin Reena, both in orange kurtas, dancing to the dhol near Girgaum. I had never danced like that in my life. I don't dance at weddings. But with thousands of people chanting, I felt like part of one huge body.
Near the bridge, the crowd got tighter. People were pushing from behind. My feet left the ground for a second. The chanting didn't stop, but it felt different now: less joy, more pressure.
Reena shouted in my ear, "Side lane. Now." We held hands and squeezed out sideways, into a narrow lane by a sweet shop.
We stood there shaking, then laughing, then quiet. We watched the idol pass from the steps instead.
I learned that belonging and safety both matter. You can love the crowd and still leave it.
- Nikita

qa.a: Into a narrow lane by a sweet shop.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling at the moment of being lifted off the ground?

Monday: The principal announced that Arjav from 10C had died in a road accident over the weekend. The hall went silent. Lalit didn't cry. He felt nothing at all, like cotton wool in his chest. He and Arjav had played on the same football team.
Wednesday: The school held a candlelight vigil in the courtyard. Parul, beside him, was sobbing. Others laid marigolds by Arjav's photo. Lalit held his candle and watched the flame, still numb. He felt terrible for not crying. Was something wrong with him?
Friday: Lalit went to the counsellor, Mrs Bose. "Everyone was crying. I just stood there."
She said gently, "People grieve differently. Some cry. Some feel numb, especially at first. Neither means you cared less."
Lalit let out a long breath. On Saturday, alone at the football ground, he cried for the first time.

qa.q: What did others lay by Arjav's photo?
qa.a: Marigolds.

qa.q: What was Lalit feeling during the vigil?
qa.a: Lalit felt numb and then guilty for not crying, worried something was wrong with him.

Manoj, you asked what I felt at that candle march. Let your Gurpreet Dadi tell you honestly.
I was sixteen. The river had flooded our town and many people died, including a boy from my class. The college organised a candle march through the bazaar. Hundreds of us, silent, holding little clay lamps.
My friends cried the whole way. I didn't. I was angry. Angry that the embankment was never repaired, angry that it took a flood for anyone to walk together. I held my lamp so tight the oil spilled on my hand.
I thought I was a bad person for feeling rage instead of sadness.

The vigil for Mr Rodrigues, the music teacher, was planned for six in the school garden. At five-thirty the rain started.
Hemant and Simran had been setting out candles in paper cups for an hour. Every time they lit one, the wind blew it out.
"This is hopeless," Simran said, wiping rain off her glasses.
Hemant didn't answer. He hadn't said much since Monday.
Students began to arrive anyway, under umbrellas. With the candles failing, someone started humming the song Mr Rodrigues had taught them for Annual Day. Others joined. Some cried. A few Class 8 boys laughed, remembering how he used to dance while conducting.
Hemant stood very still. He didn't cry or sing.
Simran moved her umbrella over him. "You don't have to do anything," she whispered.
He nodded. When the song ended, he placed his unlit cup by the photo and stood beside it until everyone left.

"Hmm." Uma tried not to smile. "I'll wave from the car. Small wave."

Then Jyoti hugged her, right there by the onions, and held on a little longer than usual.

When my best friend Urmila moved to a different school in Class 9, I acted like it was nothing. At her farewell I shrugged and said, "We'll see each other around." My classmates were there, and I didn't want to look soft.
She looked at me like she'd expected more.
For a month, we texted a bit. Short stuff. I missed her so much it made my stomach ache, and I never said it.
Then I found the comic we'd drawn together in Class 5, about two detective pigeons. I sat on my bed and read it three times.
So I wrote her an actual letter. On paper. I said, "I didn't say it at your farewell because I'm an idiot. I miss you. School is boring without you."
She called the day it arrived. She was laughing and crying. "You're such an idiot, Yusuf," she said, and I'd never been happier to be called one.

qa.q: What was the comic about?
qa.a: About two detective pigeons.

qa.q: What was Yusuf feeling during the month after Urmila left?
qa.a: Yusuf missed her so much it ached, but was too embarrassed to say it, hiding it behind short texts.

qa.q: What small step brought them close again?
qa.a: Writing an honest letter on paper saying "I miss you," which Urmila answered with a call the day it arrived.

qa.a: Urmila probably felt hurt and a little disappointed, since she expected her best friend to show some care.

grounding: The account shows a teenager hiding affection in public, then keeping the bond alive with honest written words.

Ira has this laugh that sounds like a squeaky gate. It's honestly the best laugh in the world. So I've started doing an impression of it whenever she laughs. Everyone cracks up.
The first few times she laughed too and swatted me.
Today in the canteen I did it again, and she didn't laugh. She put her hand over her mouth and went quiet for the rest of lunch. Later in class, when something was funny, she just smiled with her lips closed.
That's when I got it. She was trying not to laugh because of me.
After school I said, "Ira, the gate thing. Is it bothering you?"
She said, "A bit. Now I'm scared to laugh."
I felt awful. I told her I love her laugh, which is true, and that I'm done with the impression.
She laughed properly at the bus stop. Squeaky gate. Perfect.
- Kiran

qa.a: It suggests she felt embarrassed and self-conscious, no longer enjoying the teasing and scared to laugh.

At the tea stall by the bus stand in Ravangla, Pema and Darshan were the kings of jokes. He teased her about her bicycle that squeaked like a goat; she teased him about his hair that looked like a bird's nest. The tea-shop owner laughed along every morning.

Darshan waited for her comeback. It didn't come.
He noticed she had pulled her scarf up a little over her mouth.
"Hey," he said, quieter. "That one wasn't funny, was it?"
She shook her head.
"Sorry. Goat bicycle only from now."
Pema let out a breath. "Bird's nest," she said, and they both laughed.

Results came out the same day Jaya's whole family arrived for her cousin's wedding. The flat in Lucknow was packed, the power kept cutting, and the aunties were comparing marks before lunch.
Her cousin Dhruv had topped his school. Jaya had scraped through maths.
She went silent. When Bade Papa said, "See Dhruv, beta, learn from him," she snapped, "Great, thanks, very helpful," and walked out.
In the stairwell, her mother found her sitting on the steps. Jaya muttered, "I'm useless. Everyone thinks so."
Her mother sat beside her, sari and all, in the dusty stairwell. She didn't lecture. "I don't think so. I'm sorry that happened in front of everyone. How are you feeling, really?"
"Stupid. Like nothing I do counts."
"You count to me. Marks are one day."
She stayed with Jaya until she stopped shaking, then walked back in and quietly asked the relatives to stop comparing.

qa.a: Dhruv had topped his school.

qa.q: What was Jaya feeling when she said "I'm useless"?
qa.a: Jaya felt humiliated and hopeless about her marks, made worse by being compared to Dhruv in front of the family.

qa.q: What did Jaya's mother do that helped?
qa.a: She sat with Jaya without lecturing, apologised for the public comparison, asked how she felt, and asked the relatives to stop comparing.

For three days after the Class 10 results, Lokesh barely left his room in their Bengaluru flat. He skipped cricket. When his father, Vikas, asked about lunch, he said, "What's the point of anything?" He said it again at dinner. And again the next day.
Vikas put aside his speech about retests and tuition.
That night he knocked and sat on the edge of the bed. "You've said 'what's the point' a lot. I'm worried about you. Not the marks. You."
Lokesh's face crumpled. "I feel like I've let everyone down. Like nothing's going to get better."
Vikas stayed close. He asked, gently, whether those thoughts ever felt dangerous. Lokesh said he didn't know.
Vikas said, "Thank you for telling me. We'll get help, together," and that same night he called a helpline with Lokesh beside him. Next morning they saw the school counsellor together.

qa.a: For three days after the Class 10 results.

qa.a: Lokesh felt hopeless and ashamed, as if he had let everyone down and nothing would get better.

qa.q: Which of Vikas's choices were most important?
qa.a: Putting aside talk of marks, naming his worry, asking gently about dangerous thoughts, and getting help that same night and the next morning.

qa.a: He probably felt deeply worried and frightened for his son, which is why he acted urgently instead of lecturing.
